### Describe the bug Bug ---------- MRotaryEmbedding Triton kernel hardcodes Neox-style rotation, producing wrong results for GPT-J style models. Background ---------- MRotaryEmbedding is the multi-dimensional rotary position encoding operator used by vision-language models (e.g. Qwen2-VL, GLM-OCR). It extends standard RoPE by assigning separate position indices to temporal (T), height (H), and width (W) dimensions, enabling a single transformer to encode both text sequences and spatial image patches. Two rotation pairing conventions exist: - Neox style: pair (x[i], x[i + rotary_dim/2]) — half-split - GPT-J style: pair (x[2j], x[2j+1]) — interleaved even/odd The base class ``MRotaryEmbedding`` exposes an ``is_neox_style`` flag so that downstream kernels can select the correct pairing. Problem ------- The Triton kernel ``_triton_mrope_forward``, which is the CUDA/NPU fast-path invoked from ``forward_cuda``, hardcodes Neox-style rotation pairing and completely ignores the ``is_neox_style`` flag. When a model that requires GPT-J style rotation (e.g. GLM-4V, GLM-OCR) runs through this path, every rotary-dimension element is paired with its wrong counterpart: Expected (GPT-J): rotate(x[0], x[1]), rotate(x[2], x[3]), ... Actual (Neox): rotate(x[0], x[64]), rotate(x[1], x[65]), ... ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ incorrect pairing This silently corrupts all positional encodings. The model still runs to completion but produces garbled / nonsensical output — a failure mode that is hard to diagnose because no error is raised. Root Cause ---------- The Triton kernel ``_triton_mrope_forward`` has no parameter for rotation style; the even/odd offset calculation for GPT-J is simply missing. Bug Reproduction ------------ 1. This script compares ``forward_cuda`` (Triton kernel) against ``forward_native`` (pure PyTorch) on the same deterministic input, for both rotation styles. ```python import sys import torch from vllm.config import VllmConfig, set_current_vllm_config from vllm.model_executor.layers.rotary_embedding import mrope # the BUGGY mrope module DEVICE = "cuda" DTYPE = torch.bfloat16 # MRotaryEmbedding parameters HEAD_SIZE = 128 ROTARY_DIM = 128 MAX_POS = 16384 BASE = 10000.0 MROPE_SECTION = [16, 24, 24] NUM_TOKENS = 4 NUM_Q_HEADS = 16 NUM_KV_HEADS = 8 torch.manual_seed(42) # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Test 1: GPT-J style model — forward_cuda vs forward_native # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- print("=" * 64) print("Test 1: GPT-J style (is_neox_style=False)") print("=" * 64) with set_current_vllm_config(VllmConfig()): rope_gptj = mrope.MRotaryEmbedding( head_size=HEAD_SIZE, rotary_dim=ROTARY_DIM, max_position_embeddings=MAX_POS, base=BASE, is_neox_style=False, # ← GPT-J dtype=DTYPE, mrope_section=MROPE_SECTION, mrope_interleaved=False, ).to(DEVICE) positions = torch.randint(0, MAX_POS, (3, NUM_TOKENS), device=DEVICE) query = torch.randn(NUM_TOKENS, NUM_Q_HEADS * HEAD_SIZE, dtype=DTYPE, device=DEVICE) key = torch.randn(NUM_TOKENS, NUM_KV_HEADS * HEAD_SIZE, dtype=DTYPE, device=DEVICE) with torch.no_grad(): q_cuda, k_cuda = rope_gptj.forward_cuda( positions, query.clone(), key.clone() ) q_native, k_native = rope_gptj.forward_native( positions, query.clone(), key.clone() ) cos_sim_q = torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity( q_cuda.float().flatten(), q_native.float().flatten(), dim=0 ).item() cos_sim_k = torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity( k_cuda.float().flatten(), k_native.float().flatten(), dim=0 ).item() max_diff_q = (q_cuda.float() - q_native.float()).abs().max().item() max_diff_k = (k_cuda.float() - k_native.float()).abs().max().item() print(f"For GPT-J style, forward_cuda vs forward_native:") print(f" Query: cos_sim = {cos_sim_q:.6f} max|diff| = {max_diff_q:.4e}") print(f" Key: cos_sim = {cos_sim_k:.6f} max|diff| = {max_diff_k:.4e}") print(" → forward_cuda produced WRONG results for GPT-J style") # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Test 2: Neox style model — forward_cuda vs forward_native (sanity check) # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- print("=" * 64) print("Test 2: Neox style (is_neox_style=True)") print("=" * 64) with set_current_vllm_config(VllmConfig()): rope_neox = mrope.MRotaryEmbedding( head_size=HEAD_SIZE, rotary_dim=ROTARY_DIM, max_position_embeddings=MAX_POS, base=BASE, is_neox_style=True, # ← Neox dtype=DTYPE, mrope_section=MROPE_SECTION, mrope_interleaved=False, ).to(DEVICE) with torch.no_grad(): q_cuda_nx, k_cuda_nx = rope_neox.forward_cuda( positions, query.clone(), key.clone() ) q_native_nx, k_native_nx = rope_neox.forward_native( positions, query.clone(), key.clone() ) cos_sim_q_nx = torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity( q_cuda_nx.float().flatten(), q_native_nx.float().flatten(), dim=0 ).item() cos_sim_k_nx = torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity( k_cuda_nx.float().flatten(), k_native_nx.float().flatten(), dim=0 ).item() max_diff_q = (q_cuda_nx.float() - q_native_nx.float()).abs().max().item() max_diff_k = (k_cuda_nx.float() - k_native_nx.float()).abs().max().item() print(f"For Neox style, forward_cuda vs forward_native:") print(f" Query: cos_sim = {cos_sim_q_nx:.6f} max|diff| = {max_diff_q:.4e}") print(f" Key: cos_sim = {cos_sim_k_nx:.6f} max|diff| = {max_diff_k:.4e}") print(" → forward_cuda works correctly for Neox style") ``` Output： ``` ================================================================ Test 1: GPT-J style (is_neox_style=False) ================================================================ (some vllm INFO log...) For GPT-J style, forward_cuda vs forward_native: Query: cos_sim = 0.014274 max|diff| = 6.0312e+00 Key: cos_sim = -0.017324 max|diff| = 5.7500e+00 → forward_cuda produced WRONG results for GPT-J style ================================================================ Test 2: Neox style (is_neox_style=True) ================================================================ (some vllm INFO log...) For Neox style, forward_cuda vs forward_native: Query: cos_sim = 0.999998 max|diff| = 1.5625e-02 Key: cos_sim = 0.999997 max|diff| = 1.5625e-02 → forward_cuda works correctly for Neox style ``` 2. End-to-end: The bug can also be verified with a real GPT-J style model such as GLM-OCR (https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-OCR): a) Default eager mode (forward_cuda invoked): ```bash $ CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 vllm serve --port 8000 --tensor-parallel-size 1 --max-num-batched-tokens 2048 --trust-remote-code --enforce-eager ``` With image input, the model produces garbled / nonsensical output. b) Force forward_native via compilation config : ```bash $ CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 vllm serve --port 8000 --tensor-parallel-size 1 --max-num-batched-tokens 2048 --trust-remote-code --enforce-eager --compilation-config '{"custom_ops":["all","-rotary_embedding"]}' ``` With image input, the model produces correct output. The only difference between (a) and (b) is that (b) forces vLLM to fall back to the pure PyTorch ``forward_native`` path which correctly handles GPT-J pairing. The tricky aspect of this Triton kernel bug is that it manifests when `MRotaryEmbedding` executes via the `forward_cuda` path. However, in most production deployments, models are typically served using a compiled graph mode rather than eager mode. When the model is compiled, `MRotaryEmbedding` usually defaults to the `forward_native` path, which—by coincidence—bypasses the bug. As a result, this issue often goes undetected in real-world scenarios. For example, launching the model with the default settings (i.e., without forcing eager mode) avoids the bug and functions correctly, as demonstrated in the following command: ```bash $ CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 vllm serve --port 8000 --tensor-parallel-size 1 --max-num-batched-tokens 2048 --trust-remote-code ``` It explains why the bug remains hidden under standard deployment practices. A PR is coming soon ---------- ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.
